title: Tariffs on trial
hook: Small businesses sued, and the Supreme Court struck down the biggest tariffs of 2025. Within months, most of them were back under other laws.
notes: Court rulings: US Court of International Trade, V.O.S. Selections v. United States, Slip Op. 25-66, 28 May 2025 (three judges, unanimous); US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit (en banc), V.O.S. Selections v. Trump, Nos. 2025-1812 and 2025-1813, 29 August 2025 (7-4, per curiam; 149 F.4th 1312); Supreme Court, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229, argued 5 November 2025, decided 20 February 2026 (6-3; quotes from the official preliminary print); Court of International Trade, Oregon v. United States, Slip Op. 26-47, 7 May 2026 (2-1; injunction limited to the plaintiffs). Tariffs: Executive Orders 14193, 14194 and 14195 of 1 February 2025 (90 FR 9113, 9117, 9121) and 14257 of 2 April 2025 (90 FR 15041), all under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA); Executive Order 14389 of 20 February 2026 ending them (91 FR 9437), and CBP CSMS #67834313 (no IEEPA duties on goods entered from 24 February 2026); Proclamation 11012 (91 FR 9339) under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, 24 February to 24 July 2026; USTR, Section 301 forced-labour actions, 91 FR 47318 (28 July 2026); USTR, Section 301 action on Brazil (FR Doc. 2026-14542); Proclamations 11046-11048 under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (91 FR 46639-46663). Refunds: CIT order of Judge Richard Eaton, 4 March 2026; CBP, IEEPA Duty Refunds page (last modified 30 September 2026); CBP declaration of 15 September 2026 to the CIT as reported by Holland & Knight, Thompson Hine and Cherry Bekaert (about $166 billion of IEEPA duties on 53 million entries; about $122 billion certified and sent to the Treasury for refund by 11 September 2026). Lawsuits against the Section 301 forced-labour tariffs (argued at the CIT on 30 September 2026) were undecided as of 13 October 2026, per trade-law reports. The maps show the legal basis of the main country-wide tariff on each economy; Section 232 sector tariffs apply on top everywhere and are not shown. Dependent territories (Greenland, Bermuda, New Caledonia and others) are left blank.

scenes.title: One emergency law, almost every country
scenes.text: In 2025 the president put tariffs on nearly every country by declaring national emergencies under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), a 1977 sanctions law. China, then Canada and Mexico, were taxed over fentanyl and migration from February and March. From April almost all other countries, China included, faced 'reciprocal' tariffs of at least 10%. Older laws covered the rest: Section 232 for steel or cars, Section 301 for China since 2018.

scenes.title: Small businesses sue
scenes.text: Five small businesses, led by the wine importer V.O.S. Selections, and twelve states sued at the Court of International Trade in New York. On 28 May 2025 its three judges ruled unanimously that IEEPA does not allow these tariffs. On 29 August the Federal Circuit appeals court agreed, 7 to 4. The tariffs stayed in force while the government appealed.

scenes.title: The Supreme Court decides
scenes.text: The Supreme Court heard the case on 5 November 2025 and ruled on 20 February 2026, 6 to 3: the power to 'regulate importation' in IEEPA does not include the power to tax. Every IEEPA tariff on this map fell. Tariffs under other laws were not part of the case, and US Customs stopped collecting the IEEPA duties on 24 February.

media.text: We are therefore skeptical that in IEEPA—and IEEPA alone—Congress hid a delegation of its birth-right power to tax within the quotidian power to “regulate.”
media.by: Opinion of the Court by Chief Justice John Roberts, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 20 February 2026

scenes.title: A 150-day bridge
scenes.text: The same day, the president turned to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows a surcharge of up to 15% for 150 days to fix a balance-of-payments problem. A 10% surcharge on almost all imports ran from 24 February to 24 July 2026. On 7 May the Court of International Trade ruled it unlawful too, 2 to 1, but only for the plaintiffs who had sued.

scenes.title: Same wall, new law
scenes.text: Compare the legal basis of each country's tariff before the ruling and today.

options.label: 19 Feb 2026
options.text: The day before the ruling, almost every country's tariff rested on IEEPA, an emergency law that never mentions tariffs.

options.label: 13 Oct 2026
options.text: Today the main tariffs rest on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which lets the trade representative punish unfair practices after an investigation. Since 24 July, 60 economies pay 10% or 12.5% for failing to ban goods made with forced labour. China and Brazil pay a second Section 301 tariff. Canada also pays 50% on some goods under Section 338, a 1930 law against countries that discriminate against US goods.

scenes.title: Paying it back
scenes.text: On 4 March 2026 the Court of International Trade ordered Customs to refund IEEPA duties to all importers, not just those who sued. The refunds cover about $166 billion paid on 53 million shipments. By 11 September, Customs had sent about $122 billion, with interest, to the Treasury for payout. Refunds on the oldest entries, scheduled from 6 October, are limited to importers who sued.

media.text: The Court says nothing today about whether, and if so how, the Government should go about returning the billions of dollars that it has collected from importers. But that process is likely to be a "mess," as was acknowledged at oral argument.
media.by: Justice Brett Kavanaugh, dissenting, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump

scenes.title: Round two
scenes.text: The new tariffs are in court as well. Small businesses and 25 states have sued over the forced-labour tariffs, arguing that the trade representative stretched Section 301 beyond what Congress allowed. The Court of International Trade heard a test case on 30 September 2026 and, as of 13 October, had not ruled. The Section 232 tariffs on steel, cars and medicine still stand.
